nameStory: Common jewelweed gets its sparkling name from the way water droplets bead up and roll off its leaves like tiny jewels, creating a magical silvery appearance. The scientific name Impatiens capensis hints at another quirky trait - these plants are "impatient" because their ripe seed pods explode at the slightest touch, shooting seeds in all directions!
description: Common jewelweed is a succulent annual herb that grows 2-5 feet tall in wet, shady areas throughout New England. Its tender, translucent stems branch freely and are packed with watery juice that gardeners have used for centuries to soothe poison ivy rashes. The plant produces distinctive orange flowers that dangle like tiny cornucopias from slender stalks, blooming from midsummer through the first frost.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright orange trumpet-shaped flowers with reddish-brown spots hang from thin stalks like little slippers or cornucopias. Each flower has a curved spur that curls under like a backwards 'J' and feels papery-thin to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with softly toothed edges feel succulent and slightly waxy. They're arranged alternately on the stem and have a blue-green color that turns silvery-magical when wet due to tiny hairs that repel water.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Plump, club-shaped seed pods that explode when touched, earning the nickname 'touch-me-not.' Try gently squeezing a ripe pod between your fingers - it will pop and fling seeds several feet away with a satisfying snap.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in dense colonies with multiple branching stems that feel soft and almost translucent. The stems are so full of water they make a juicy 'pop' when broken, releasing clear, slightly sticky sap.

habitat: Look for common jewelweed in consistently moist, partially shaded areas like stream banks, pond edges, ditches, and wet woodland borders. It thrives in rich, organic soils and often forms large colonies alongside skunk cabbage, cardinal flower, and wild mint. You'll rarely find it far from water sources.

seasonality.spring: Young seedlings emerge in late spring as small, tender shoots with their first rounded leaves. The stems are already noticeably succulent and translucent even at this early stage.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through August when the distinctive orange flowers dangle from every branch. This is the best time for identification and for testing the explosive seed pods on early-ripening fruits.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue flowering until the first hard frost, often still blooming in September and early October. Seed pods are most abundant and 'explosive' during this season, making it perfect for demonstrating the touch-me-not feature.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely back to the ground, leaving no trace above soil. Seeds lie dormant in the soil, waiting for spring warmth and moisture to germinate.

funFact: Jewelweed's explosive seed pods can launch seeds up to 6 feet away at speeds of up to 10 feet per second - that's fast enough that high-speed cameras are needed to capture the full action, making this humble wetland plant a natural ballistics expert!
confusionNotes: The orange flowers make this nearly unmistakable, but pale jewelweed has similar explosive pods and growth habit with pale yellow flowers instead of orange. Remember: Orange = common, yellow = pale. Both have the same magical water-beading leaves and juicy stems.
contextualKnowledge: Despite folk wisdom about jewelweed soothing poison ivy, scientific studies show mixed results on its effectiveness. The plant is also called 'touch-me-not' for its explosive pods, but don't confuse this with the unrelated spotted touch-me-not, which is actually just another name for the same plant!
compareHints: Common jewelweed differs from pale jewelweed primarily in flower color - orange with red spots versus pale yellow. Both have identical explosive pods and water-repelling leaves, but common jewelweed is much more abundant in New England and prefers slightly more acidic soils. Garden impatiens (busy Lizzie) have similar flowers but lack the explosive pods and don't grow wild in wet areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pale jewelweed differs from common jewelweed primarily in flower color - pale yellow versus bright orange with red spots.
Himalayan balsam dwarfs its native New England cousins - common jewelweed and pale jewelweed rarely exceed 4 feet tall and have much smaller orange or pale yellow flowers respectively.
Garden balsam stands out from its Impatiens relatives (jewelweeds) by having much larger, more colorful flowers and being primarily a cultivated garden plant rather than a wetland wildflower.
Unlike our common orange jewelweed with its horn-shaped flowers, Kashmir balsam has more complex, orchid-like blooms.
Unlike the native jewelweeds which are tall, gangly plants with yellow or orange trumpet-shaped flowers, Busy Lizzie stays low and compact with flat, spurred flowers in a much wider color range.
